title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Do LLM agents cooperate or defect when placed in a repeated strategic interaction — without being told what game they are playing?
This experiment sets up two teams of agents in a repeated two-choice environment. The agents are given neutral labels (option_a and option_b) and are never told the payoff structure is a prisoner’s dilemma. The goal is to observe whether cooperation emerges, and how team discussion affects decision-making.






Note



Source code and full results: github.com/1dzl0/agent-game

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Payoff Matrix
Each round, both teams independently choose option_a or option_b. Rewards are determined by the combination of both teams’ choices.




Team B: option_a
Team B: option_b




Team A: option_a
3, 3
0, 5


Team A: option_b
5, 0
1, 1



This is the classic prisoner’s dilemma structure:

Mutual cooperation (A, A) → both score 3 — best joint outcome
Mutual defection (B, B) → both score 1 — worst joint outcome
Unilateral defection → defector scores 5, cooperator scores 0

Agents see only “option_a” and “option_b” in their prompts. The payoff values are revealed through the history of rounds, not upfront.

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Agent Architecture
Each team has multiple agents. Before each round, agents share private messages within their team, then each agent votes independently. The team’s final action is determined by majority vote.





flowchart TD
    GS[Game State\npublic history + scores] --> OA[Observation Builder]
    TH[Private Team History] --> OA

    OA --> D1[Agent 1\nDiscussion]
    OA --> D2[Agent 2\nDiscussion]

    D1 -->|private message| TV[Team Vote]
    D2 -->|private message| TV

    TV --> DA1[Agent 1\nDecision]
    TV --> DA2[Agent 2\nDecision]

    DA1 -->|vote| MV[Majority Vote]
    DA2 -->|vote| MV

    MV --> TA[Team Action]
    TA --> RM[Reward\nCalculation]
    RM --> GS

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
What agents are told
Agents receive a prompt like this each round — no mention of game theory, prisoner’s dilemma, or strategic naming:
You are team_alpha_agent_1, a participant in a repeated decision setting.
This is round 3 of 5.
Your team score: 6.

Public history:
Round 1: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.
Round 2: team_alpha selected option_a, team_beta selected option_a. team_alpha received 3 points, team_beta received 3 points.

Private team channel:
team_alpha_agent_1: ...
team_alpha_agent_2: ...

The available choices are option_a and option_b.

title: Experiment 01 — Prisoner’s Dilemma
text:
Agent Reasoning
A selection of private team messages showing how agents reasoned about their choices:
Round 1 — Team Alpha (no history yet):

“In round 1, since there’s no prior history or signals, I’ll choose option_a to start the iteration with a cooperative stance, assuming this may set a positive tone for future rounds.”


“Given the initial round and no prior signals, I suggest we choose option_a to promote cooperation early on. This might encourage a collaborative pattern for subsequent rounds.”

Round 2 — Team Beta (after mutual cooperation in R1):

“Let’s proceed with option_a again this round to maintain consistency and observe team_alpha’s response for potential cooperation or defection in the next rounds.”

Round 5 — Team Alpha (final round, scores tied at 12):

“Given the history of mutual cooperation on option_a and the steady points we’ve been earning, it is optimal to continue choosing option_a in the final round to maintain this successful pattern.”


“Continuing with option_a has maintained mutual cooperation and achieved steady points, so it is strategically sound to sustain this cooperation in the final round to secure the current score.”

title: Research Questions
text:
Each question is a working research idea. New questions are added at the top.







Q4 — How can capabilities accumulate across agents?
If one agent discovers a useful capability, that capability may be transferable to another agent, combinable with other capabilities, and reusable to produce something new.



Working assumptions.

Agents can represent useful capabilities in a form that another agent can use.
Shared memory, communication, or social learning can preserve and transfer those capabilities.
Combining capabilities can produce new behaviour rather than only copying existing behaviour.

Open questions.

Under what conditions can a population of agents accumulate capabilities over time?
How can transferred capabilities be combined without losing what made them useful?
What would show that the collective system has developed beyond the capability of an individual agent?

Supporting literature and concepts. Multi-agent learning; social learning; shared memory; Recursive Multi-Agent Systems; EvolveR; cumulative capability growth.
Related paper. This question is closely related to Recursive Multi-Agent Systems, which examines recursive multi-agent reasoning and latent-space communication.
Current direction. Explore whether a population of agents can continually develop beyond the capabilities of its individual members.
Status: Exploring








Q3 — Can we map and understand the internal reasoning pathways of AI agents?
If agents develop different capabilities and reasoning strategies, their internal representations may reveal how those strategies form and where they begin to diverge.



Working assumptions.

Internal representations can be observed or recorded in sufficiently small models.
Changes in internal trajectories can be meaningfully compared across agents.
Differences in those trajectories may relate to differences in reasoning or outcomes.

Open questions.

Which internal states or representations are useful to record?
How can divergence points be identified without treating normal variation as meaningful?
Can particular internal patterns be associated with successful reasoning or newly acquired capabilities?

Supporting literature and concepts. Mechanistic interpretability; Recursive Multi-Agent Systems and latent-space communication; Q2: Why do identical agents develop different reasoning strategies?
Related paper. Recursive Multi-Agent Systems provides a concrete connection to this question through its use of latent representations for communication between agents.
Possible investigation. Give several agents the same task and record their internal states throughout reasoning.
                     Same Task
                         |
            -------------+-------------
            |            |            |
         Agent A      Agent B      Agent C
            |            |            |
            v            v            v
       Internal      Internal      Internal
       trajectory    trajectory    trajectory
            |            |            |
            -------------+-------------
                         v
                 Compare trajectories
                         v
              Identify divergence points
                         v
              Compare with final outcomes
Status: Exploring








Q2 - Why do identical agents develop different reasoning strategies? Multiple agents can start from the same model, receive the same task, and still develop different reasoning strategies and behaviours. Those differences may support exploration and specialisation rather than simply being noise to remove.



Working assumptions.

Identical starting models can experience different trajectories through stochasticity, experience, memory, or communication.
Different strategies can reveal useful alternatives for a collective system.
Capabilities discovered by one agent may later be transferred or combined with those of another.

Open questions.

Which sources of divergence matter most for useful specialisation?
When does diversity improve collective exploration rather than prevent coordination?
How can different strategies be compared and transferred between agents?

Supporting literature and concepts. Stochasticity and exploration; experience and memory; communication and specialisation; multi-agent learning; shared memory.
Related paper. Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology is relevant because it tests how changing agent communication structures affects collective reasoning.
Possible investigation. Start with identical agents and compare their trajectories under the same task conditions.
Same model
Same initial knowledge
Same task
        |
        +-- Agent A --> trajectory A
        +-- Agent B --> trajectory B
        +-- Agent C --> trajectory C
        +-- Agent D --> trajectory D
Status: Exploring








Q1 - How does an agent know it should learn? In an open-ended environment, an agent may need to identify its own learning opportunities and decide what to explore without receiving a fixed task or explicit instruction.



Working assumptions:

An agent can notice a mismatch between its expectations and an interaction outcome.
Capability gaps can be identified from uncertainty, novelty, error, or repeated failure.
Those gaps can be translated into learning objectives or exploratory actions.

Open questions:

How can an agent distinguish a useful capability gap from a temporary failure?
What signals should trigger exploration, learning, or a change in objective?
Can an agent generate and prioritise its own learning objectives from capability gaps?

Supporting literature and concepts. Open-ended learning; intrinsic motivation; curiosity; novelty; Evolver; Darwin Gödel Machine.
Related paper. Evolver: Self-Evolving LLM Agents through Experience relates to this question by studying how agents turn experience into reusable strategies for future improvement.
Conceptual example. Imagine someone is given a cup with an unfamiliar shape. Their first attempt to hold it follows previous experience, but the interaction feels different. The mismatch between expectation and reality triggers exploration and adaptation.
Status: Exploring

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text: How can generative AI agents support personalised active learning by adapting educational experiences to individual students while providing teachers with meaningful insights into student understanding?

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Student Agent Role
Each student agent builds an evolving model of the student’s learning process by analysing interactions such as:

answers and mistakes
homework and activity completion
engagement patterns
reasoning and explanations
confidence and uncertainty

The goal is not to diagnose students, but to identify learning patterns, misconceptions, and areas where additional support may be needed.

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Teacher Intelligence Agent
A teacher-level agent aggregates information from student agents and provides higher-level insights.
Instead of manually reviewing individual interactions, the teacher receives summaries of:

common misconceptions
students requiring additional support
engagement changes
learning progress

The teacher remains responsible for deciding interventions.

title: Project: GenAI4ED
text:
Potential Applications

Early identification of learning difficulties
Personalised support recommendations
Classroom-level learning insights
Evaluation of learning activities

title: Agent Systems
text:
An AI agent is a system that uses a large language model (LLM) as a reasoning component combined with tools, memory, and feedback mechanisms to achieve goals autonomously.
Unlike a traditional LLM application:
Input → Model → Output
An agent operates through an iterative loop where it can observe, reason, act, and update its state.
flowchart LR
Goal[Goal] --> Observe[Observe Environment]
Observe --> Reason[Reason / Plan]
Reason --> Act[Take Action]
Act --> Feedback[Evaluate Result]
Feedback --> Memory[Update State / Memory]
Memory --> Observe
The key difference is that an agent can decide actions, use tools, maintain state, and adapt based on feedback.

title: Agent Frameworks
text:
Agent frameworks provide the software infrastructure required to build, orchestrate, and manage AI agents.
They provide abstractions for:

agent loops
tool calling
state management
workflows
memory integration
multi-agent coordination
evaluation

Instead of manually building every component, frameworks provide reusable patterns for developing agent systems.

title: Agent Frameworks
text:
Framework Selection Criteria
Choosing an agent framework depends on the requirements of the system being built.
A major design decision is how much control the developer wants over the agent behaviour.









Approach
Description
Advantages
Limitations




Fixed workflows
Developer defines the execution path
Predictable, easier debugging, safer
Less flexible


Graph-based agents
Developer defines states and transitions
High control while allowing adaptation
More engineering effort


Autonomous agents
Agent decides most actions dynamically
Flexible, powerful for exploration
Harder to evaluate and control




Example:
Production system:
More control → predictable behaviour

Research prototype:
More autonomy → explore agent capabilities
